title: The three-minute limit on 78s
summary: Disc jockeys and jukeboxes demanded under three minutes.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: One thing that was a big factor, I'm sure, was that you were writing pieces that had to fit on one side of a 78.

Yes, everything you did had to have a limit and more than that, disc jockeys wouldn't play it unless it was two fifty--they wanted it less than three minutes or else it interfered with the commercials. Also in those days jukeboxes were a big thing and they wanted to make it for the jukebox.
I'm sure it was especially crucial in the case of those pieces, because you weren't just taking a pop tune and writing two to three choruses
In other words, did you feel restricted in any way or hampered in the way you wrote those because they had to be a specific length?

No. I think if you begin to do too much of them you begin to think that way. If you write too many commercials you begin to think in terms of thirty seconds of the minute, but barring that, you can write a concise piece of music in three minutes, and sometimes better than if you take thirty to forty. I've heard a lot of thirty and forty minute pieces that shouldn't be that at all. They should stop abruptly at three minutes.
